summary: Redwood AE + SE walked NovaCommerce through an edge-cases demo focusing on long-context handling, high TPS scenarios, streaming backpressure, and timeout/fallback behaviors. Customer is exploring a Dedicated or Private deployment for production traffic; wants to run a benchmark/pilot. Key asks: security docs, runbook for streaming backpressure, and a small dedicated pilot to validate latency at 1k TPS with long (32k token) contexts.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (NovaCommerce CTO), Marco Diaz (NovaCommerce ML Eng), Sara Khan (NovaCommerce Platform), Unassigned (Speaker 5)
Links shared: deck https://redwood.ai/edgecases-deck, runbook link (priv) https://redwood.ai/kb/streaming-backpressure, benchmark template (sheet) https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/template

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya Raman, our solutions engineer. Quick run through agenda, we'll demo the Console & API, then Priya will hit the deep-dive on long context and streaming behaviors, and we'll finish with Q&A and next steps.

[00:32] Evelyn: Thanks, Jordan. Quick context, we at NovaCommerce are building a real-time product summarization and personalization pipeline; main concerns are long user histories (we're looking at 20k-40k token contexts), and we expect bursts up to 1k TPS during sales events. Security is a blocker - SOC2 and KMS integration.

[01:05] Jordan: Totally. Priya, quick overview?

[01:12] Priya: Sure. I'll start in the Console to show model catalog, routing policies, and then the API demo for streaming with a simulated long context. Important: our runtime supports KV cache + prefix caching and we have quantization-aware variants for cost. Small note, auto-transcript may say "KV cash" sometimes, that's just the ANA.

[01:40] Marco: Quick Q, when you say 40k tokens, is that end-to-end memory or do you do sliding windows or KV cache?

[01:55] Priya: Good call. We have a few options - native long-seq model variants we optimize for, plus an explicit KV cache that stores previous key/values to avoid re-running the entire context. For your use-case we typically combine prefix KV caching and sliding windows for older history; the runtime stitches them. Subject to model architecture constraints though.

[02:25] Jordan: We'll demo both patterns. Also we'll be honest about tradeoffs - long context increases latency and memory, so we show fallbacks and graceful degradation.

[02:50] Priya: Demo time — opening the Console. (screen share) Here is the Route config: policy rules for latency vs cost. For NovaCommerce you can pin a Dedicated fleet, but also configure 'region fallback' to hosted variants if capacity's tight.

[03:30] Priya: Now API demo — I'm going to stream a simulated 32k token context. Note: transcription may mangle some function names, e.g. "streaming backpresser" — it's backpressure.

[03:58] [03:58] Priya: (begins stream) Sending initial handshake, then continuous tokens — you can see per-chunk timings in the Console. We set chunk_size=2048 to show progressive outputs.

[04:30] Marco: Are those chunks assembled client-side or you handle reassembly?

[04:37] Priya: We provide ordered streaming frames; your client can reassemble with the chunk ids. We also have an SDK that auto-reassembles and manages reconnects.

[05:06] Evelyn: What happens under heavy TPS? If we push 1k TPS with lots of streams, do you start dropping connections or queue?

[05:18] Priya: Good question. For streaming we expose a few knobs — per-connection window limits, tenant-level concurrency. Under sustained excess, we apply backpressure signals in-band (HTTP 429 with Retry-After) and queue in the dedicated request router; we also have an elastic burst pool for Dedicated customers. Note that under extreme oversubscription we recommend fallback policies that route to a cheaper, lower-context variant.

[05:55] Jordan: Also we can configure 'soft timeouts' — if response isn't available in X ms we return the partial tokens + a confidence flag and optionally invoke a synchronous lower-latency model.

[06:20] Marco: Is that part of the SDK or server side?

[06:27] Priya: Server-side orchestration with client hooks. The SDK just surface the events.

[07:02] Priya: I'm going to run a small load simulation — 200 concurrent streams, each with a 32k-ish context, to show the tail latency. (runs test) Console metrics show median P95 and P99 in the chart.

[07:35] [07:35] Priya: You can see P50 ~ 210ms per token, P95 spikes at 1.6s per chunk when KV is cold. After KV warms, the P95 reduces significantly.

[07:55] Marco: That "KV cold" behavior — what's the warmup cost and how long does it last?

[08:05] Priya: Depends on access patterns; warm-up is typically the cost of populating KV per session, often 1-3 requests depending on your prefix size. We strongly recommend pre-warming for flash events via a warm-up plan we can script.

[08:32] Unassigned (Speaker 5): Is there a cost penalty for KV retained memory?

[08:38] Jordan: There is memory/retention cost as part of the Dedicated pricing model; we show that in the pricing template. We'll send a breakdown.

[08:50] Evelyn: Security: KMS integration — do you support customer-managed keys and HSM? Also audit logs?

[08:58] Jordan: Yes. Private deployments support HSM and KMS; Dedicated supports customer KMS via integration. Audit logs and per-token tracing can be turned on for compliance (note increased storage). We'll attach SOC2 docs and architecture notes.

[09:20] Marco: About timeouts — what's the recommended client-side timeout vs server soft timeout? We've had issues with the client getting half the stream then reconnecting and duplicate outputs.

[09:33] Priya: We recommend idempotent streaming patterns with check-pointing: each chunk has sequence IDs so your client can resume from last ack. Server soft timeout defaults to 90s for hosted but can be tuned for Dedicated/Private. For long contexts you may want longer soft timeouts but pair with early partial returns to keep UX responsive.

[10:05] Sara: Any best practices for handling partial outputs? e.g., the UX should show "partial" state?

[10:12] Priya: Exactly. We suggest showing partial text with 'confidence' metadata and a clear 'complete' flag. Our SDK surfaces these flags.

[10:28] Jordan: Quick interjection — competitor note: some vendors just drop streams silently; we surfaced explicit 429 and Retry headers which customers said helps.

[10:42] Evelyn: Can we see the failure modes? Like a simulated timeout and fallback to a smaller model?

[10:50] Priya: On it. (runs simulation) Triggering a configured timeout at 5s to show fallback. Here we have route policy: primary=long-context-large, fallback=low-latency-medium.

[11:12] [11:12] Priya: You can see the partial tokens returned with confidence=low and then a follow-up from the fallback model. Logs show the routing decision and latency chain so you can debug.

[11:35] Marco: How much quality drop when you fallback? Any way to rerank or merge outputs?

[11:42] Priya: We support reranking and structured output merging. We also support a 'roll-forward' policy where the fallback returns a short summary and we kick off an async job to recompute with full context and update downstream stores.

[12:05] Evelyn: For our use case, consistency is important — can't have two different answers across subsequent requests. How do you preserve determinism?

[12:15] Priya: Determinism is tough with sampling. We advise seeding + temperature=0 for deterministic outputs or using a canonical reranking step. For longer contexts the rerank step is the best approach for consistency.

[12:40] Jordan: Back to pricing and Dedicated: we'll propose a 30-day pilot with a small reserved fleet, run your 1k TPS load tests in staging, and validate latency/throughput. The pilot includes access to our ops channel and runbook.

[12:58] Marco: For the 1k TPS test, can Redwood simulate both streaming and non-streaming? We need both.

[13:06] Priya: Yes. We'll provide the benchmark harness (it's the sheet we linked) and can run server-side tests if you grant a temporary staging token.

[13:30] Evelyn: On Private deployment: we have strict data residency and need on-prem option. How quickly can that be provisioned?

[13:41] Jordan: On-prem takes longer — typical timeline 8-12 weeks for initial deployment + compliance review. VPC/private cloud is faster, usually 3-6 weeks. We'll enumerate the required infra and security checklist.

[14:05] Marco: Any special considerations for your runtime on air-gapped networks?

[14:11] Priya: We ship a hardened on-prem bundle, with offline image sync and KMS connectors that can use internal HSMs. Some telemetry is disabled by default; we provide an audit kit.

[14:34] Unassigned (Speaker 5): Do you support multi-tenant isolation within a Dedicated fleet?

[14:40] Priya: Yes, strong tenancy boundaries; Dedicated gives you reserved nodes and per-tenant encryption. We can show the RBAC controls in the Console.

[15:02] [15:02] Priya: Now, a more realistic high-TPS streaming stress — I'm going to ramp to 800 TPS steady with 1k bursts. Watch the backpressure signals and the queue length dashboard.

[15:25] Priya: Ramp in progress... at 600 TPS we see increased queueing at the ingress, at 820 burst many clients receive 429 with Retry-After 5s — our router engages the burst pool.

[15:45] Marco: Do you shed load or throttle gracefully per customer? We can't have noisy neighbors affecting other routes.

[15:53] Priya: For Dedicated you get tenant-isolated resources; for hosted we use fair-share scheduling with per-route quotas and preemptible burst pools. In either case we can configure per-route SLOs.

[16:18] Jordan: Note: if you need absolute isolation during campaigns, Dedicated with pinned capacity is recommended.

[16:30] Evelyn: How do you recommend we instrument our clients to handle 429 + partial streams? We want minimal duplicated outputs.

[16:40] Priya: Best practice: use chunk-sequence IDs, ack processed chunks, implement idempotent dedupe at the application layer keyed by request-id + sequence range. We'll include a reference implementation in the SDK.

[17:05] Marco: Are there limits to sequence ID length or chunk count? We have very long sessions.

[17:12] Priya: Sequence IDs are 64-bit; chunk count is configured per route but practically you won't hit protocol limits before resource constraints.

[17:35] Unassigned (Speaker 5): What's the expected storage footprint for tracing 7 days of traffic at 1k TPS?

[17:45] Jordan: It depends on event detail, but rough estimate: if you enable full per-token traces it's X GB/day per 1k TPS; with sampling or aggregated traces you can reduce significantly. We'll send a sizing doc.

[18:05] Priya: I'm going to show the failure logs — the trace shows the timeout, routing decision, and fallback. (shares) You can filter by request-id.

[18:35] Marco: Can we hook those traces into our SIEM?

[18:41] Jordan: Yes, we support log forwarding to S3/Blob and direct SIEM integrations.

[18:55] Evelyn: On data retention and PII, we need options to redact or not store sensitive data.

[19:03] Priya: You can configure redaction pipelines, or opt for no-storage mode where only ephemeral tokens are processed and nothing is persisted. For auditing you can use hashed variants.

[19:30] Marco: About quantization — you've mentioned quant-aware variants. How does that affect quality for long-context models?

[19:38] Priya: Quantization reduces memory for large models and can affect quality slightly for some tasks; we provide validation profiles per model/version so you can see delta vs baseline. For heavy-context scenarios we often recommend mixed-precision or 4-bit quantized kernels that we benchmark per workload.

[20:02] Jordan: Quick pause — any other security blockers?

[20:08] Evelyn: SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, plus role-based access for Console. Also wants per-route audit trails.

[20:18] Jordan: Supported. We'll attach implementation notes and sample SAML metadata.

[20:35] Priya: Going to simulate a client reconnect scenario where half the stream is delivered and then client reconnects. This demonstrates resume semantics. (runs)

[21:00] [21:00] Priya: The client reconnected and resumed from chunk 153; the SDK handled reassembly and dedupe. Logs show no duplicated final artifact.

[21:25] Marco: Nice. For the pilot we'll likely want to run exactly this pattern.

[21:32] Evelyn: About costs — what's the unit pricing for long-context tokens vs standard tokens?

[21:40] Jordan: We bill on token-equivalent compute. Long context implies more compute and higher unit price; Dedicated pricing uses reserved capacity plus usage tiers. We'll send a model-specific price sheet.

[21:58] Unassigned (Speaker 5): Do you do token compression or storage-optimized encodings?

[22:05] Priya: We have prefix compression options and we also support payload compression over the wire; they don't change model tokenization but reduce network overhead.

[22:28] Marco: Any gotchas with large prompt sizes and streaming chunk boundaries? We've seen mis-splitting of structured JSON outputs across chunks which breaks parsers.

[22:38] Priya: We handle chunk boundary tokens and include meta markers so structured outputs can be reassembled safely; we recommend sequence-aware JSON parsers or the SDK helper which reconstructs and verifies JSON before returning to the app.

[22:58] Jordan: Quick reminder — we'll send the benchmark harness and pricing; Priya will share the backpressure KB and runbook.

[23:12] Evelyn: Could you include a list of expected metrics we should expect to see during a campaign?

[23:20] Priya: Yes — P50/P95/P99 latency per chunk, token throughput, queue depth, 429 rate, retry-after distribution, KV hit rate, model-switch rate, and error rates. We'll include Grafana dashboards.

[23:45] Marco: For the 1k TPS test, what's a realistic expected P95 for a warmed KV long-context workload?

[23:54] Priya: On a Dedicated pinned fleet with warmed KV, P95 per chunk typically in the 300-600ms range depending on model size. We'll run your exact prompts in pilot to validate.

[24:15] Unassigned (Speaker 5): When would you recommend using async jobs vs streaming for our use-case?

[24:24] Priya: If you can tolerate eventual consistency and want lower peak compute impact, async is good: client submits job, you get a callback when result is ready. For interactive UX streaming is preferred but more sensitive to bursts.

[24:48] Jordan: Let's cover SLOs briefly — Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers we can contract. Hosted has best-effort with published performance profiles.

[25:05] Evelyn: Do you provide runbooks for incident response?

[25:12] Jordan: Yes — incident runbooks and a dedicated pager channel for pilot customers. Priya will share.

[25:30] Priya: I'm going to trigger an induced error to show how the system surfaces root cause. (runs) Error traces show model OOM at worker 7, auto-retry policy engaged and request routed to alternate worker.

[25:58] Marco: How many retries before you shift to fallback? Can that be tuned?

[26:06] Priya: Tunable; default is 2 retries then fallback; we can tune per-route.

[26:20] Jordan: We're approaching the end. Any last questions?

[26:28] Evelyn: Timeline question — we'd like to start pilot ASAP. If we sign next week, can you provision dedicated trial in under two weeks?

[26:36] Jordan: For a small pilot yes, typically 7-14 days if infra approvals are quick. Private/on-prem longer.

[26:50] Marco: For the benchmark, we'll provide traces and prompts. How do you want those?

[26:57] Priya: Anonymized request traces in the sheet format we shared. Also note any PII fields so we can configure redaction.

[27:15] Evelyn: Ok, last ask: share SOC2 and the KMS integration guide.

[27:22] Jordan: Will do. We'll email the docs and pricing by Thursday.

[27:40] [27:40] Priya: Quick recap demo highlights: long-context via KV + model variants, streaming with chunking and resume semantics, behavior under 800-1k TPS with backpressure and explicit 429s, timeout and fallback demo, and security options (KMS, HSM, audit).

[28:05] Jordan: Next steps recap: Jordan send pricing and contract draft; Priya send runbook & configs; Marco to provide traces & prompts; schedule follow-up check-in 2026-02-24.

[28:22] Evelyn: Sounds good. Thanks both.

[28:28] Marco: Thanks.

[28:30] Unassigned (Speaker 5): Thanks everyone.

[28:35] Jordan: Thanks, talk soon.

[28:40] -- End main demo --

[28:50] Post-meeting quick notes:
- Customer emphasized deterministic outputs and avoidance of duplicate responses in reconnect flows.
- Priority asks: SOC2 + KMS, pilot to validate 1k TPS with 32k contexts, and runbook for streaming backpressure + SDK sample for chunk resume.
- Potential blockers: internal procurement SLA and on-prem timeline if they choose Private.

[29:30] System notes (auto-gen): transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" instead of KV cache; "backpresser" instead of backpressure). Speaker attribution may be imperfect for non-Redwood attendees.
